5.51.m: Śeṣa said: / Having heard that speech of Suratha from the mouth of Aṅgada, / all those expert in battle, mounted on chariots, readied themselves for war.
There arose the sound of drums, and likewise the beat of kettle-drums; / roaring shouts of the heroes burst forth upon the battlefield.
With the rattling sounds of chariots and the trumpeting of elephants, / all that world was pervaded, and a great roar reached the heavens.
Filled with enthusiasm for battle, the heroes skilled in war / made diverse sounds terrifying to a coward.
While such an uproar was going on, the king named Suratha, / surrounded by his sons and soldiers, marched out to the battlefield.
Filling the earth with elephants, chariots, horses, and hosts of infantry, / he appeared to the warriors as if flooding it like an ocean.
Resounding with the blare of conches and likewise with cries of victory, / seeing him eager for battle, the king said to Sumati:
Śatrughna said: / "This king has arrived, surrounded by a mighty army. / In this situation, what is our duty? Tell me that, O wise one!"
Sumati said: / "Here the fight should be waged by many warriors skilled in battle, / by Puṣkala and others who are fiercely formidable and expert in all weapons and missiles.
Let the son of the Wind, possessed of supreme valor, / exceedingly mighty and skilled in opposing combat, fight with the king."
Śeṣa said: / While the prime minister was speaking thus, just then the king's sons, / arrogant, stretched their bows upon the battlefield.
Seeing them, the mighty warriors Puṣkala and others, fierce in combat, / advanced on their chariots, holding bows and arrows in their hands.
The mighty hero Puṣkala, skilled in supreme weapons, / fought in single chariot combat against the illustrious great hero Campaka.
The son of Janaka, Kuśadhvaja, fought Mohaka; / Vimala fought Ripuñjaya; Subāhu fought the irresistible [warrior];
Pratāpāgrya [fought] with Pratāpin, and Aṅgada with Balamoda; / Nīlaratna with Haryakṣa, and Satyavat with Sahadeva;
the mighty King Vīramaṇi fought with Bhūrideva; / and powerful Ugrāśva fought with Asutāpa.
The experts in warfare fought a great duel from chariots, / all of them skilled in weapons and missiles, all of them adept in battle.
When the battle had thus begun with the sons of Suratha, / an extraordinary slaughter took place there, O best of sages!
Puṣkala said to Campaka: "What is your name, O king's son? / Blessed are you who have entered into the midst of battle with me!
Now stand! Why do you flee? How could your life remain? / Come, fight with me, O you who are skilled in all weapons and missiles!"
Hearing what was spoken by him, that mighty prince, / the hero, addressed Puṣkala in a voice deep as a thundercloud:
Campaka said: / "This battle here will not be won by name or by lineage; / nevertheless, I shall tell you my name, preceded by my strength.
The lord of the Raghus is considered my mother; Rāghava is my father; / Rāmacandra is my kinsman; Rāghava is my own relative.
My name is Rāmadāsa, ever a servant of Rāma; / Rāma, who is merciful to devotees, will deliver me in battle.
Adopting the perspective of the world, I tell you now: / I am the son of Suratha, and Vīravatī is my mother."
My name is that which makes everything delightful in the spring month; / infatuated by the honey, bees forsake this abode of nectar.
In color it resembles gold, bearing in its center a linga-like form; / by that appellation, O hero, know my captivating name!
Fight with your arrows in battle! For who indeed is able to conquer me? / Now I shall show my marvelous prowess.
Śeṣa said: / Having heard these grand words, Puṣkala was pleased in his heart; / deeming him invincible, he began discharging arrows in battle.
He advanced toward Puṣkala, who was letting loose a multitude of arrows by the millions; / then Champaka, filled with fury, strung his bow.
He loosed sharpened arrows that rent asunder the ranks of the enemy, / marked with his own name and fitted with gold-feathered shafts.
The mighty hero Puṣkala shattered them on the battlefield, / discharging rock-sharpened arrows all around, casting darkness with arrows.
Seeing his own arrows severed by the hero, Champaka, / filled with rage, challenged the powerful Puṣkala:
Saying, "Do not flee abandoning the fight!" once again in battle, / he swiftly struck Puṣkala in the chest with ten arrows.
Ah, those arrows of exceedingly swift flight, having reached / Puṣkala's chest, struck him forcefully and drank his copious blood.
Agonized by those arrows, the hero took up five arrows / with extremely sharp tips, in great fury, warding them off like mountains.
Those arrows of his and the other's, exceedingly mighty, / fashioned in the sky, were split into a hundred pieces by the prince.
Having cut down those arrows with extremely sharp tips, the powerful son of Suratha / fitted a hundred arrows to strike Puṣkala in the heart.
Those arrows, shattered into a hundred fragments by the high-souled Puṣkala / and beaten back by the speed of his shafts, fell on the battlefield's edge.
Then, seeing that exceedingly great feat, the king's powerful son / struck him squarely in the chest with a thousand arrows.
Puṣkala, skilled in the highest weapons, quickly cut them down as well; / yet again [Champaka] swiftly fitted ten thousand arrows to his bow.
Puṣkala, skilled in the highest weapons, quickly cut them down as well; / then, exceedingly enraged, [Champaka] unleashed a rain of arrows.
Recognizing the oncoming shower of arrows, Champaka, slayer of heroes, / struck Puṣkala as he was praising him, saying, "Bravo! Bravo!"
Puṣkala, seeing Champaka endowed with mighty valor, / fitted the missile of Brahmā to his bow, he who was skilled in all weapons.
The great missile discharged by him blazed across the ten directions; / pervading the sky, heaven and earth, it prepared to bring about the destruction of the universe.
Seeing that missile loosed, Champaka, expert in all weapons, / discharged that very same missile to neutralize it and destroy his advancing foe.
The people regarded the united splendor of the two as cosmic dissolution; / then missile neutralized missile, the rival missile becoming united [with it].
Seeing that marvelous deed, Puṣkala said, "Halt, halt!" / and in anger struck Champaka with unfailing arrows.
Disregarding those loosed arrows, the magnanimous Champaka / then loosed the terrible weapon of Rāma against Puṣkala.
Seeing that missile loosed by the high-souled Champaka, / as soon as he set his mind to cutting it down, he was seized by the arrow.
Bound by the heroic Champaka and placed on his chariot, / the magnanimous one then resolved to send him to the city.
There arose a great cry of despair when the one named Puṣkala was bound; / the warriors fled, bent on running away toward Śatrughna.
Seeing them broken, Śatrughna spoke to Hanūmat: / "By which hero has my army, adorned with valiant warriors, been broken?"
Then [he] said: "O lord of the earth, having bound Puṣkala, / this heroic Champaka, proud in his position, slayer of enemy heroes, is carrying him off."
Hearing such words, Śatrughna, filled with anger, / said to the son of the wind: "Quickly release him from the prince!
From his powerful son who has captured the warrior Puṣkala, / release him, O foremost of heroes! How can you stand [idle] in battle?"
Hearing these words, Hanūmat said, "So be it," / and went to release Puṣkala from the warrior Champaka.
Seeing Hanūmat arriving to release him, / [Champaka], incenser of enemies, struck him with hundreds and thousands of arrows.
He quickly broke those arrows discharged by that high-souled one; / once more, unleashing arrows at him swiftly, he became formidable.
He crushed all those iron arrows loosed by the enemy; / seizing a sāl tree in his hand, he struck the prince.
The powerful one chopped that hurled sāl tree into pieces like sesame seeds; / an elephant was then hurled by Hanūmat at the prince's head.
Struck by Champaka, that too fell dead upon the earth; / Hanūmat, skilled in supreme weapons, then hurled boulders.
Champaka completely pulverized all those boulders in an instant / with an arrow-machine, O brāhmaṇa—this was a great wonder!
Seeing all those boulders hurled by him shattered, the son of the wind / grew exceedingly angry in his heart, mindful of his immense valor.
Approaching and seizing him in his hand, the monkey sprang into the sky; / swift-moving, he went far above the reach of sight.
Remaining in the sky, Champaka fought with Hanūmat; / in a great bout of hand-to-hand combat, the best of monkeys was struck.
The hero, formidable as a mountain of pride, was enraged in mind; / seizing Champaka by the foot, he dashed him to the surface of the earth.
Struck down by the king of monkeys, rising up swiftly in an instant, / he seized Hanūmat by the tail and whirled him all around.
The king of monkeys, witnessing his strength, laughed and seized him again by the foot; / having whirled him around a hundredfold, he hurled him down before an elephant.
The very powerful prince Champaka fell to the ground / unconscious, adorning the battlefield rich in heroic ornaments.
Then Champaka's followers cried out in distress, "Alas, alas!"; / and [Hanūmat] freed Puṣkala, who was bound by Champaka's noose.

5.52.m: Śeṣa said: / Seeing Champaka fallen, the powerful kṣatriya Suratha, / his body overwhelmed with grief for his son, advanced standing in his chariot.
Suratha, filled with anger, endowed with mighty power, / letting loose a rush of heavy breaths, then challenged the king of monkeys.
Seeing the king challenging him, the heroic lord of monkeys, / the mighty hero, advanced toward him with great speed.
As Hanūmat approached, treating mighty champions as mere straw, / King Suratha addressed him in a deep voice resembling a raincloud.
Suratha said: / "Blessed are you, foremost of monkeys, possessing mighty power and valor, / by whom a great service for Rāma was performed in the city of the rākṣasa!
You are a devoted servant of Rāma's feet; / by you, a hero, my powerful son Champaka has been felled.
Now, having bound you, I shall go to my city; / stand firmly, O lord of monkey kings, for what I have declared is true!"
Hearing what was spoken by Suratha, the lord of monkeys / spoke with a steady voice on the battlefield adorned only by heroes:

Hanūmān said:
“You are one who remembers Rāma's feet; we are Rāma's servants. / If you bind me by force, my master will release me.
O hero, fulfill the true promise that lies in your heart! / Remembering Rāma indeed, one goes to the end of sorrow; this the Vedas say.”

Śeṣa said:
Having praised the son of the wind who was speaking thus, Suratha / pierced [him] with many terrible arrows, whetted on a grindstone.
Disregarding those released arrows that caused blood to flow, / [the monkey] seized in his hand [Suratha's] bow, strung and fitted with an arrow.
Having seized the bow with both hands, the enraged monkey broke it, / screeching, terrifying the heroes, and tearing warriors to pieces with his claws.
Seeing his bow with its bowstring broken by him, / [Suratha] took another great bow adorned with a string.
The monkey angrily seized that bow as well and broke it. / [The king] took another bow, and the very mighty one broke that.
Even when that bow was broken, he took up another bow. / Endowed with great speed, he swiftly broke that bow as well.
In this way, eighty bows of the king were shattered, / while at every moment [the monkey] uttered roars in many ways out of great wrath.
Then, utterly enraged, [the king] took up a fierce spear. / Struck by that spear, the eager hero fell down for a moment.
Having stood up, furiously enraged, he seized the king's chariot / and, taking it, flew up with immense speed toward the ocean.
Seeing him flying up, Suratha, the slayer of enemy heroes, / struck the rising son of the wind on his chest with iron maces.
The chariot released by him was crushed to powder from afar in an instant. / Mounting another chariot, [Suratha] swiftly went after the son of the wind.
Enwrapping that chariot with his tail on the field of battle, / Hanūmān smashed it together with its horses, charioteer, and banner.
Mounting another chariot, the very powerful king advanced. / His limbs enraged, the son of the wind swiftly smashed that chariot.
Seeing that chariot broken, Suratha mounted another; / that too was suddenly smashed by him, along with horses and charioteer.
In this way forty-nine chariots were broken by Hanūmān. / Seeing that deed, even the king was astonished, along with his soldiers.
Enraged, he said to the lord of monkeys: “Blessed are you, O son of the wind! / No one has performed or will perform this heroic deed!
Wait for a single moment while I string my bow, / O son of the wind, O bee at the lotus-feet of Rāma!”
Having said this, stringing his bow, filled with rage, / he fixed the missile named Pāśupata upon a terrible arrow.
Then spirits, Vetālas, Piśācas, and Yoginī-headed beings / suddenly appeared, terrifying the son of the wind.
The monkey was seen by all people bound by the Pāśupata weapon. / While they were saying, “Alas, alas!”, the son of the wind,
remembering Rāma in his mind, snapped [the bonds] at that very moment. / With his limbs suddenly freed, he fought with King Suratha.
Seeing his limbs freed, Suratha, knower of supreme weapons, / deeming him to possess immense strength, took up the Brāhma weapon.
The son of the wind, laughing, swallowed the powerful Brāhma weapon. / Seeing it swallowed, the king, the ruler of the earth, remembered Rāma.
Remembering Rāma, the son of Daśaratha, he set the Rāma-weapon upon his bow / and said to him: “You are bound, O foremost of monkeys!”
No sooner had he heard that and began to move, than the hero Hanūmān, / Rāma's servant, was bound on the battlefield by the king using the Rāma-weapon.
Hanūmān said to the king: “What can I do, O ruler of the earth? / I am bound by the weapon of my master, not indeed by any ordinary one.
Therefore I respect it, O king; take me to your city! / My master, that ocean of compassion, will come and release me.”
When the son of the wind was bound, the enraged Puṣkala went toward the king. / As that Puṣkala was advancing, [Suratha] pierced him with eight arrows.
The mighty one struck the king with many thousands of arrows; / many of his arrows were cut down by the king on the battlefield.
Thus, while Suratha and Puṣkala were both enraged in battle, / the whole world, stationary as well as moving, was covered with arrows.
Seeing their preparation for battle, the celestial armies were bewildered; / what mention then of human beings, who instantly fell into terror?
With the discharges of weapons and counter-weapons, sanctified by great mantras, / there occurred a tumultuous battle that made the hair of heroes stand on end.
Then the enraged king took up an iron shaft; / but that was cut down by calf-tooth-tipped arrows loosed in anger along with Bhārata [weapons].
When that arrow was cut down, the king angrily took up another; / before he could cut that arrow down, it struck him, wounding him in the chest.
Puṣkala of great splendor fell into a faint; / having fought a very great, wondrous battle with the king, the high-minded one [swooned].
When Puṣkala fell, King Śatrughna, the tormentor of foes, / standing on his chariot, advanced, furious against Suratha.
Rāma's brother of great strength said to King Suratha: / “A great deed has been done by you in that the son of the wind was bound.
The great hero Puṣkala also, and my other soldiers / of great strength and valor, have been brought down in terrible battle.
Now stand firm! Having struck down my heroes on the battlefield, / where will you go, O ruler of the earth? Endure my arrows!”
Having heard this speech of the hero, the mighty Suratha, / holding the beautiful lotus-feet of Rāma in his heart, replied:
“I have brought down in battle your heroes with the son of the wind at their head; / now I shall strike you down as well on the battlefield.
Remember Rāma, the hero who comes in person to protect [his own]! / Otherwise there is no life for you before me, O tormentor of foes!”
Having spoken thus, the king struck him with thousands of arrows; / he placed Śatrughna completely within a cage formed by a multitude of arrows.
Against him who was releasing a mass of arrows, Śatrughna loosed the fire-weapon / in order to burn up those straight-jointed arrows.
Seeing that weapon loosed, the great King Suratha / quenched it with the Vāruṇa weapon and pierced [Śatrughna] with crores of arrows.
Then [Śatrughna] fitted onto his bow the wondrous weapon given by the Yoginī, / which stupefies all heroes and brings on sleep.
Seeing that great stupefying weapon, the king, remembering Hari, / spoke to Śatrughna, he who was skilled in all arms and missiles:
“To me, who am already enchanted by the remembrance of glorious Rāma, / no other bewilderment appears, nor brings me fear or distress.”
When that hero had spoken thus, he released that great missile; / severed by that arrow, it fell upon the battleground.
Seeing that great stupefying weapon rendered fruitless against the king, / [Śatrughna], filled with extreme astonishment, fitted an arrow to his bow,
by which Lavaṇa, the crusher of great Asuras, had been slain; / he set that terrible arrow, radiant like glowing fire, upon his bow.
Seeing it, the king said: “This arrow strikes the heart of the wicked; / in front of a devotee of Rāma, it does not even shine.”
Yet as he was speaking thus, the slayer of foes with that arrow / swiftly pierced his heart that shone like a blazing fire.
Afflicted with pain by that arrow, seized by great agony, / that scorcher of foes fainted for a moment on the chariot's floor.
Passing through that pain in an instant, he spoke to the enemy before him: / “Endure one blow of mine! Where are you going before me?”
Having spoken thus in the great battle, he fitted an arrow to the bow, / its body encircled with a wreath of flames and fitted with golden feathers.
That arrow, released from the bow, was blocked on its path by Śatrughna, / yet though cut, its front point swiftly struck his heart.
Fainting from that arrow, he fell upon his chariot. / Then a cry of woe arose, and the entire army broke and fled.
Suratha, the servant of Rāma, attained victory in battle; / ten heroes, struck unconscious by his ten sons, lay fallen somewhere.

5.53.m: Śeṣa said: / Sugrīva, seeing that army broken on the battlefield / and his master unconscious, went towards the king to fight.
“Come, O king! Having rendered all of us unconscious, where / are you going? Quickly give battle to me, O expert in war!”

Having spoken thus, having uprooted a large tree with its branches, / he, possessed of might, struck him on the head with force.

By that blow, the exceedingly mighty king, / having seen Sugrīva, then upon his own bow—
having fitted sharp arrows, angrily / struck him on the chest with extreme valor, being mighty.
Laughing, Sugrīva swiftly shattered all those arrows, / and that very mighty one struck Suratha in the chest.
With mountains and peaks, and with trees as big as elephants, / tearing Suratha with his claws, he struck him impetuously.
He too quickly bound him with the terrible missile named Rāma; / bound, the foremost monkey recognized Suratha as a servant of Rāma.
Just as an elephant, having received an iron chain hanging from its leg, / can do nothing at all, so indeed did he become.
Victory was won by that great king Suratha, who had good sons; / placing all the heroes on his chariot, he went towards his own city.
Having arrived in the assembly hall, the illustrious king said to the bound son of the Wind: / “Remember the venerable lord of the Raghus, compassionate, the protector of devotees,

so that that very wise one may instantly release you from captivity; / otherwise I will not release you from captivity even in ten thousand years!”

Hearing what was said, the son of the Wind then, / seeing himself tightly bound, and the heroes
fallen unconscious, afflicted by the strikes of the enemy's arrows, / remembered [Rāma] for liberation from bondage:

The glorious Rāmabhadra, born in the lineage of Raghu, the husband of Sītā, lotus-petal-eyed, / compassionate, he remembered with all his faculties, freed from grief, for his own release from bondage.

O destroyer of the distress of devotees, wearing an enchanting form, / release me immediately from bondage; do not delay!

"Indeed, by you the foremost elephants and others were freed, / and the gods being severely burned by the fire of the demon race.

the braid of hair resting on that beautiful woman’s head / was untied; O abode of mercy, remember me!

You are devoted to the work of sacrifice with the foremost lords of sages; / you deliberate on dharma, O one whose feet are praised by kings!

Here today I am bound with tight bonds by Suratha; / release me quickly, O Great Puruṣa, O God!

If you do not release [me] now from this intensity of remembrance, / O you whose lotus feet are worshipped by the best of all the gods!"
the world will exultantly laugh at you on this account; / therefore make no delay here; release me quickly!”
Hearing this, the Lord of the Universe, hero of the Raghu line, an ocean of compassion, / set out on the swiftly speeding Puṣpaka to deliver his devotee.
Adorned by his follower Lakṣmaṇa and by Bharata, / accompanied by crowds of sages headed by Vyāsa, the monkey saw him.
Seeing his lord arrived, he said to the king: / “Behold, O king, Hari has arrived through compassion to release his own!
Formerly many servants of his own were freed upon remembering [him]; / similarly, he has come to free me who was bound by a snare.”
Seeing the glorious Rāmabhadra arriving, Suratha instantly, / overflowing with a flood of devotion, bowed hundreds of times.
The four-armed Lord Rāma embraced his devotee with his own arms, / repeatedly sprinkling his own head with tears of joy.
He said: “Blessed is your body! A great deed was done by you! / Hanūmān, the lord of monkeys, powerful in every way, was bound by you.”
Lord Rāma released that foremost of monkeys from captivity; / looking with his gaze, he revived all those unconscious warriors.
Looked upon by Rāma who is served by gods, they abandoned their fainting fit; / arisen, they beheld the charming, glorious Rāmabhadra.
Bowing to the lord of the Raghus, asked by him of their health, / having become happy, the royal heroes reported all their well-being to the king.
And Suratha, seeing Rāma come to show grace to his own servant, / gladly surrendered his entire kingdom together with the horse.
He pleased the glorious Rāma with numerous services; / he said: “An injustice was done by me; forgive it, O Rāghava!” / Then Lord Rāma said to him: “Protection of the horse was performed by you;
this is the duty of Kṣatriyas, that one fights alongside the master. / By you an auspicious deed was done; the heroes were pleased in battle.”
Worshipping the man-lion who had spoken thus, that son remained; / the glorious Rāma, having stayed for three days and taken leave of him, departed.
together with the sages in the aerial chariot that moves at will. / Seeing him, they were amazed and told delightful stories of him.
Having established Campaka in his own city, the mighty Kṣatriya Suratha, / of great strength, set his mind on going along with Śatrughna.
Śatrughna, having regained his horse, caused the kettle-drums to sound; / he had varied blasts of conches sounded everywhere.
Together with Suratha, the hero released the sacrificial steed; / it roamed across other lands, and no mighty one seized it.
Wherever the steed went, roaming here and there, / there Śatrughna and Suratha went with a vast army.
At one time, on the bank of the Jāhnavī, he arrived at the excellent hermitage of Vālmīki, / frequented by foremost sages, marked by morning smoke.

5.54.m: Śeṣa said: / Having gone to perform the morning rites, Lava, the son of Jānakī, accompanied by the sages' sons, / went to fetch sacrificial wood fit for those rites.
There he saw the sacrificial horse, marked with a gold tablet, / perfumed with the divine fragrance of saffron, agallochum, and musk.
Seeing it, filled with curiosity, he said to the sons of the sages: / 'Whose steed, swift as thought, has by fate reached my hermitage?
Come with me, look at it, do not be afraid!' / Having said this, Lava quickly approached the steed.
That scion of Raghu's lineage stood near the horse, / holding a bow and arrows on his shoulder, difficult to conquer like Jayanta.
Going with the sons of the sages, he read the excellent tablet / situated upon its forehead, shining with rows of clear letters:
'Great is the lineage of Vivasvat, renowned in all worlds, / wherein no one harms others nor covets the wealth of others.
The banner of the Solar dynasty, archer, master of initiation into archery, a venerable lord, / whom all gods along with the immortals revere with jeweled crests—
his son, who removes the pride of heroes' might, upholder of the Raghus, / is the fortunate Rāmacandra, the crest-jewel of all heroes.
His mother was born a jewel, the daughter of the king of Kośala; / the jewel born from her womb is Rāma, the destroyer of foes.
Well-instructed by a brāhmaṇa, he performs a horse sacrifice / to remove the sin of slaying the eminent brāhmaṇa named Rāvaṇa.
By him has this foremost of steeds, fit for sacrifice, been loosed, / surrounded by a mighty host, well protected by trenches.
Its protector is my brother Śatrughna, slayer of Lavaṇa, / accompanied by an army composed of hosts of elephants, horses, chariots, and foot-soldiers.
If any king has such proud conceit arising from his own arrogance: / "We are heroes, we are the best among bowmen, we are formidable here,"
let them seize by force this steed, adorned with garlands of gems, / swift as thought, rushing at will, radiant with all paces.

Then my brother Śatrughna will easily, by force, free it / from one afflicted by calf-tooth-headed arrows shot from his bow.'

"Those kṣatriyas who are born of a kṣatriya maiden / and in good fields and families of the noble..."
may seize it; those of the contrary nature / must bow down, having surrendered their kingdom to Rāghava.'
Having deliberated thus, Lava, enraged, seizing his weapons and bow, / spoke to those sons of sages, his speech stammering with fury:
'Behold at once the insolence of this kṣatriya, / of this king who wrote the might of his own prowess on the forehead-tablet!
Who is this Rāma? Who is Śatrughna? They are worms relying on petty strength! / Were they born in a family of kṣatriyas, and not we, the noble ones?
Is the mother who bore this hero Jānakī, and not the mother of Kuśa, / who bore that jewel named Kuśa, just as the fire-drill bears fire?
Now I will display kṣatriya status and the rest in every way! / If this slayer of foes is indeed of kṣatriya lineage,
he will take the steed, fit for the sacrificial rite, bound by me; / otherwise, having abandoned his kṣatriya duty, he will worship Kuśa's feet.
Now he shall be put to sleep by arrows discharged from my bow, / along with the other mighty heroes who adorn the battle arena!'
Uttering such words, Lava seized that horse, / treating all the kings like straw, an excellent bearer of bow and arrow.
Then the sons of the sages said to Lava, who was eager to take the horse: / 'Rāma, king of Ayodhyā, is possessed of great might and prowess.
Even Indra, proud of his own strength, would not seize his steed. / Do not seize it; listen to this beneficial word of mine!'
Keeping in mind what was said, he said to the sons of the twice-born: / "You do not know the strength of kṣatriyas, O best of the twice-born!"
Kṣatriyas are proud in heroism; the twice-born are distinguished in eating. / Therefore, go home and eat what is brought by your mother!'
Addressed thus, they fell silent, watching that prowess; / those sons of the sages stood outside at a distance from Lava.
While this event was occurring, the attendants of that king / arrived, and seeing that horse bound, they then said to Lava:
'Who bound the horse? Aha! At whom is Dharmarāja enraged? / Who, surrounded by a shower of arrows, will suffer the ultimate agony?'
Then Lava said at once: 'The excellent horse has been bound by me! / Whoever releases it, against him my elder brother, the great Kuśa, will be enraged.
What will Yama do even if that lord comes himself? / Having bowed down, he will quickly depart, well-pleased by a rain of arrows!'
Śeṣa said: / Hearing this speech, saying 'He is just a boy,' / those who had come to release Hari's bound horse,
even those attendants of Śatrughna who had arrived to release it, / [he attacked]: grasping his bow in both hands, he discharged razor-faced arrows.
Their arms severed, out of grief they went back to Śatrughna; / when questioned, they all reported the cutting off of their arms by Lava.

5.55.m: Vyāsa said: / Having heard this delightful story of the mighty Lava, the sage, / having doubts, questioned the thousand-faced serpent.
Glorious Vātsyāyana said: / 'Formerly it was said by you that Rāma, longing for his wife, / abandoned Sītā alone in the forest because of the slanderous words of a washerman.
Where were the two sons born to Jānakī? Where did they attain archership? / And how was that science learned by him who seized Rāma's horse?'
Vyāsa said: / Hearing this word of the sage, the serpent Śeṣa, highly intelligent, / praised the brāhmaṇa and spoke the wondrous story of Rāma.
Śeṣa said: / Rāma ruled the kingdom in Ayodhyā together with his brothers, / protecting the entire division of the earth righteously alongside his wife.
Sītā bore his semen; five months had passed at that time. / The queen shone exceedingly, like the threefold Veda bearing the Supreme Spirit.
Once at that time, Rāma asked the daughter of Videha: / 'What pregnancy longing do you have, virtuous lady? It shall surely be fulfilled by me.'
Being thus questioned in secret, the chaste woman, bashful before her husband, / spoke nectarous words to Rāma, her voice trembling with modesty:
Sītā said: / 'By your grace, everything has been enjoyed by me and will be enjoyed auspiciously; / no worldly object is lacking in my mind, O beloved!
She whose husband is like you, whose noble feet are praised by the gods— / she has everything; nothing at all remains [to be desired].
Since you persistently ask me about a pregnancy longing residing in my mind, / I tell you the truth before you, O charming husband:
A long time has passed since I, truly, saw Lopāmudrā and the other women; / my mind is eager, O husband, to see those beautiful ladies.
Having attained the kingdom with you, established in manifold pleasures, / I would be ungrateful if I did not intend to pay homage to them at some time here.
Having gone there, I would honor those treasures of asceticism with garments and other things, / and I would also offer shining gems and ornaments.'
So that they, being pleased, may bestow charming blessings upon me. / This is my pregnancy craving, beloved; fulfill what is in my heart."
Hearing these extremely charming words of Sītā, / Rāmabhadra, exceedingly pleased, said to his beloved:
"You are fortunate, daughter of Janaka. In the morning you shall go to the ascetics rich in penance; / having seen them and achieved your purpose, you shall return to my side."
Hearing these words of Rāma, she experienced supreme joy: / "In the morning, indeed, I shall have the sight of the female ascetics."
Then that night, spies were sent by Rāma to observe / the reports heard about his fame; and at midnight they went softly forth.
They, hearing the delightful stories of Rāma every day, / went on that day to the grand house of a wealthy man.
Seeing a burning lamp and hearing human speech, / the spies stood there for a moment and heard [his] great renown.
There a fair-eyed woman, delighted, / spoke very charming words to her infant suckling at her breast:
"Drink my sweet milk as much as you wish, my son; / later it will be very difficult for you to obtain, my child!
Rāma, radiant as the petal of a blue lotus, is the lord of this city; / for the people residing in his city there will indeed be no rebirth.
Since there is no rebirth, how could there be drinking of breast milk on earth? / Therefore drink this breast milk again and again, thinking in your heart that it is rare.
For those who remember Śrī Rāma, meditate upon him, and speak of him, / there will never again be any drinking of milk."
Having heard such words, the nectar of the glorious Rāma's fame, / delighted, they went to another house of a fortunate person.
Meanwhile, another spy, considering that charming house, / stood there for a moment out of a desire to hear Rāma's renown.
There a beautiful woman, chewing betel affectionately given / by her husband, who was resting comfortably upon a couch,
adorned with the lovely tinkle of bracelets, perfumed with camphor and aloe, / looked at her husband with flickering eyes and said to the handsome man:
"My lord, you appear to me just like the lord of the Raghus, / possessing an exceedingly beautiful, very delicate body.
Possessing eyes reaching the edges of lotus petals, an enchanting, broad chest, / and arms adorned with armlets, you are Rāma himself to me!"
Hearing these charming words of his beloved, / making the corners of his eyes dance, handsome as Kāma, he spoke:
"Listen, beloved! What you have spoken as a virtuous wife is very charming. / That is fitting for devoted wives, for one's own husband is indeed Rāma.
Yet where am I, ill-fated, and where is Rāma, the greatly fortunate one? / Where am I, insignificant as an insect, and where is he, worshiped by gods such as Brahmā?
Where is a firefly, and where is the sun, jewel of the sky? Where is a base moth? / Where is the lion, king of beasts, enemy of elephants, and where is the dull-witted hare?
Where is that divine river Jāhnavī, and where is the foul gutter-water in the street? / Where is Meru, the abode of gods, and where is an insignificant heap of guñjā seeds?
Just so, where am I, and where is that Rāma, by the dust of whose feet a woman / turned to stone instantly assumed a form that enchanted Brahmā?"
She embraced her husband as he spoke these words; / aroused with passion, ravished by love, she made her bow-like eyebrows dance.
Having heard such words, he went to another dwelling; / then another spy heard words filled with fame.

A certain woman, having prepared a bed of flowers, sandalwood mixed with camphor,
and everything suitable for love, said to her husband:

“Husband, take your rest on this flower-couch fit for pleasure,
with applications of sandalwood ointment and many varied delights.

Men like you alone are worthy of enjoyment, not those who turn away from Rāma;
enjoy in full measure everything attained by Rāma's grace.

A loving wife like me, sandalwood cooling all fever,
this couch prepared with flowers—all has arisen from Rāma's grace.

Those who will not worship Rāma cannot even fill their own bellies,
deprived of clothing, enjoyment, and all else.”
To the woman speaking thus, her delighted husband said: / "Everything you say is true; it comes about through Rāma's grace to me."
Having thus heard the fame of the auspicious Rāma, the spy departed; / then another spy staying at another person's house heard [these] words:

A woman, intent on playing the vīṇā on a couch with her beloved,
singing the noble renown of Rāma with her lover, said to her husband:

“Husband, we are most blessed, whose master and lord of the city
is Śrī Rāma, our protector, who protects his subjects like sons.

He who performed a great deed, difficult to accomplish and not easy:
he subdued the ocean and built a bridge across it;

Having slain his enemy Rāvaṇa and sacked Laṅkā with the monkeys,
he brought back Jānakī—here he performed a great conduct!”
Hearing the words spoken with sweet syllables, / her husband smiled at her and then spoke these words again:

“O enchanting lady, this is indeed a great deed of Rāmacandra,
such as the slaying of the ten-headed [Rāvaṇa] and the subduing of the ocean.

Having come to earth in sport when prayed to by Brahmā and the gods, that great one
performs virtuous deeds that remove great sins.

Do not consider Rāma, who brings joy to Kausalyā, a mere mortal;
having assumed human form in sport, he creates, protects, and destroys this universe.

Blessed are we who behold the lotus face of Rāma,
which is difficult even for the gods, Brahmā and the rest, to see; we have accumulated great merit!”

He listened to the deeds of Rāmacandra that bring joy to the ears;
standing repeatedly at the door, the spy heard these and other words.

Another went to yet another house and stood there to hear Hari's fame;
there too he heard the glorious renown of Rāmabhadra.

Playing dice with her husband, a very charming woman
spoke sweet words, as if making her bracelets dance:

"Everything has been won by me quickly, my dear; / what will you do, O one whose mind captivates?"

Having playfully spoken these and other words,
she embraced her husband in joy.

Her husband said: “Fair-limbed lady, well-adorned one, I have indeed won;
for me who ever remember Rāma, there is defeat nowhere.

Now I shall defeat you, remembering enchanting Rāma,
just as of old the gods, remembering [him], defeated the sons of Diti in an instant.”

Having spoken thus, he made a throw of the dice;
thereupon he won, and delighted, he said:

“What I said has come true; you in your fresh youth are defeated!
One who remembers Rāma will never have fear from an enemy.”
As the two of them were speaking thus to one another with eagerness, / embracing firmly with affection, the spy then went home.

Thus the five great spies, having heard the king's renown,
praising him among themselves, joyfully went each to his own home.

A single spy, the sixth, observing the houses of the artisans there,
went, wishing to hear the renown of the king, the lord of the earth.

A washerman, touched by fury, with red eyes, denounced
and kicked his wife who had stayed in another's house:

“Go from my house to his house where you stayed for the day!
I will not accept you, a wicked woman who transgresses my word.”

Then his mother said: “Do not abandon her who has returned home,
free from fault and untouched by wicked action!”

Then the washerman, filled with rage, replied to his mother:
“I am not like Rāma, to accept a beloved who has stayed in another's house!

Whatever that king does may indeed be considered righteous,
[but] I will not take a wife who has stayed in another's dwelling!”

Again and again he said this: “I am not Rāma, the lord of the earth,
who [accepted] Jānakī, who had stayed in the house of another, his demon foe!”
Hearing these words, the spy, overcome with fury, / seized his sword in his hand and resolved to kill him.

Then he remembered what Rāma had said: “No subject of mine is to be put to death.”
Knowing this, the noble-minded one checked his fury.

Afflicted with great sorrow upon hearing that, he went from there, enraged,
sighing repeatedly, to where the five spies were staying.

Having gathered together there, they related to one another
the deeds of Rāma that they had heard, worshipped by all the worlds.

Hearing what he spoke, they deliberated among themselves:
“This unmentionable thing spoken by a wicked man must not be told to Raghunātha.”
Deliberating thus, they went to their houses and slept, eager, / intent on their purpose: 'In the morning we shall offer praise to the king.'

5.56.m:
Śeṣa said:
In the morning, having performed his daily rites and gratified the Brāhmaṇas
who were foremost knowers of the Veda with gifts of gold according to rule, he went to the assembly.

All the people went to the court to bow down to Raghunātha, the lord of the earth,
who protected all his subjects like sons.
Lakṣmaṇa held the parasol over the head of the king, / while Bharata and Śatrughna both held a pair of chowries.

The sages, headed by Vasiṣṭha, sat near in attendance there,
as did the ministers, dispensers of justice, headed by Sumaṃtra.

When the session had thus commenced, those six spies, well-adorned,
arrived to bow down to the ruler of men who sat in the assembly.

Seeing those spies wishing to speak, the best of kings,
eager [to hear], entered a private chamber inside the assembly hall.

In private the wise king questioned all those spies:
“Tell me truly, O subduers of foes,

What do the people say of me? What of my wife?
What do the people say of my ministers, and how do they describe their conduct?”
Having heard his words, the spies then spoke to Rāma, / to the lord of the Raghus who was inquiring with a voice deep as a thundercloud.
The spies said: / "O lord, your fame purifies all people on earth now; / in house after house it was heard by us, praised by men and women.
The great lineage of Vivasvat has been adorned by you, the supreme lord, / who descended to earth; your fame has spread far and wide.
Many mighty rulers such as Sagara were famous, / but their fame was not like yours.
With you as lord, all the subjects have been fulfilled; / for them there is no untimely death, nor affliction from diseases and passions.
Just as the moon in the world, just as the river Jāhnavī, / even so your good fame illumines the earth.
Hearing of your fame, Brahmā and the other gods are deeply astonished. / O lord, everywhere your fame purifies people now.
We who are your spies, O king, are the most blessed of all; / from moment to moment we gaze upon your charming countenance."
Observing such speech from the five spies, Rāghava / questioned the sixth spy, whose face was marked by embarrassment.
Rāma said: / "Speak the truth, O man of great intellect, what was heard among the mixed crowds. / Report to me all of it as it was spoken; otherwise you incur sin and other faults."
Again and again Rāma asked him quickly and in detail; / nonetheless he did not speak to Rāma the words spoken by the people.
Then Rāma said in return to that spy whose face was marked by dismay: / "I adjure you by truth! Report everything exactly as it occurred."
Then the spy spoke to Rāma in a very slow voice: / "Though unfit to be spoken, the words uttered by an artisan must be told to you."

The spy said: / "Master, everywhere is your fame concerning the slaying of the ten-headed Rāvaṇa and other deeds; / yet elsewhere [there is talk] regarding your wife who stayed in the demon's house, alas!
An artisan, a washerman, seeing his wife at midnight / after she had stayed in another's house, reviled her and beat her.
His mother said to him: 'Why do you beat this faultless woman? / Take your wife back; do not revile her; act according to my word.'
Then that washerman replied: 'I am not King Rāma, / who took back Sītā though she had lived in the demon's house!
Every action done by a king becomes righteous, O lord, / while the deed even of other righteous actors is considered unrighteous!'
Again and again he said: 'I am not King Rāma!' / I was enraged at that time, O king, remembering your command:
'Cutting off his head right then, I will dash it to the ground!' / But then I reflected: 'Where is Rāma, and where is a washerman?'
This wicked man speaks falsehood; this being spoken is not the truth. / If you command, O Rāma, I shall kill him at once.
Though it should not be uttered, it has been told to you due to your insistence on this report. / The king is the ultimate authority here; let him deliberate on what is fitting."
Śeṣa said: / Hearing these words, whose syllables were like mighty thunderbolts, / sighing and drawing repeated gasps, he fell unconscious.
Seeing the king unconscious, the spies were overcome with sorrow; / they fanned him with the tips of their garments to remove his distress.
Regaining consciousness in a moment, the king said to them: / "Go quickly to Bharata and send him to me!"
Those spies, sorrowful, swiftly went to the house of Bharata; / conveying the message, they reported Rāma's word.
Hearing Rāma's message, wise Bharata immediately went to the palace, / and hearing that he was in private, went with haste toward Rāma.
Approaching, the noble-minded one asked the doorkeeper: / "Where is that noble Rāma, my brother, the ocean of mercy?"
The heroic [Bharata] went to the gem-adorned house pointed out by him; / seeing Rāma dejected, fear entered his mind:
"Has Rāma become angry, or what is this grief of the lord?" / Then he spoke to the king, who was sighing again and again.
"O Lord, whose face is usually easy to delight, why is it downcast? / It appears through tears like the moon whose body is seized by Rāhu.
Tell me truly the whole reason. What can I do for you? / Cast off your sorrow, O great king! How can you be a vessel of grief?"
Being addressed thus by his brother in a voice choked with emotion, / the heroic and righteous Rāmacandra spoke to his brother:
"Listen, brother, to my words—the cause of my sorrow! / O wise brother, wipe it away today, this very morning!
In the solar dynasty of Vaivasvata, no king was ever wounded by disgrace; / but today my fame has become tarnished, as the Gaṅgā joined by the Yamunā.
Only those men on earth who have fame live well; / but the life of those wounded by ill-repute is just like that of corpses.
Those who have renown on earth possess eternal worlds; / but may there be a fall to the depths for those bitten by the serpent of dishonor!
Today my fame, celebrated across the world like the heavenly river, has been sullied. / Hear what was said today by a washerman!
In this city today, a washerman spoke words of reproach concerning Jānakī. / Therefore, brother, what should I do on the face of the earth?
Should I abandon myself today, or should I abandon this woman Jānakī? / Tell me truly, what ought to be done by me regarding both?"
Having spoken thus, shedding tears, his limbs trembling and agitated, / the spotless crest-jewel of the righteous fell to the ground.
Seeing his brother fallen, Bharata, filled with sorrow, / watched over Rāma and gently restored him to consciousness.
Seeing that Rāmacandra had regained consciousness, though sorely grieved, / he spoke these very charming words to dispel his sorrow:
"Who is this wretched washerman? What reproachful word did he speak? / I will cut out the tongue of him who utters reproach against Jānakī!
Then Rāma recounted the words that came from the mouth of the washerman, / which had all been heard by the spy, to the high-souled Bharata.
Hearing that, Bharata said to his brother who was grieving with sorrow: / "Jānakī was purified by fire in Laṅkā and worshipped by heroes.
Brahmā declared, 'She is pure,' and so did your father Daśaratha. / How can she, who is revered by the world, be abandoned because of the words of a washerman?
Your fame, extolled by Brahmā and the gods, purifies the worlds. / How could it indeed become tarnished today by the speech of a washerman?
Therefore, cast off this great sorrow born of the reproach against Sītā! / Rule the kingdom together with her, the fortunate one who is now pregnant!
How can you wish to abandon your own splendid body? / Without you, the destroyer of our grief, all of us are ruined today!
Without you, that most glorious Sītā would not live even for a moment. / Therefore, let her, devoted to her husband, enjoy abundant prosperity with you!"
Hearing these words of Bharata, the righteous [Rāma], / best among those who know how to speak, addressed these words once again:
"All that you say, brother, is endowed with righteousness. / Nevertheless, carry out by my command the word that I speak:
I know she was purified by fire, holy, and revered by the world; / yet frightened of public censure, I am abandoning my own Jānakī.
Therefore, taking in your hand a sharp, dreadful sword, / sever my head! Or else abandon my wife Jānakī in the forest!"
Hearing these words of Rāma, Bharata fell / to the ground in a swoon, his body trembling, full of tears.

5.57.m: Vātsyāyana said: / "How did the Lord, whose good fame purifies the world, / bring about the utterance of reproach against Jānakī? Tell me that, O you of noble vows!

O Śeṣa, act in such a way that great joy may arise in my mind! / When drinking the nectar that has flowed from your mouth today, there is only that satisfaction by which worldly existence is cut asunder."
Śeṣa said: / "In the great city of Mithilā, there was a king named Janaka; / in that [city] he ruled well, delighting his subjects with righteousness.
As he, Sīradhvaja, was plowing the ground with a plowshare whose tip was long, / there emerged an exceedingly beautiful maiden.
Then King Sīraketu, having attained immense joy, / gave the name Sītā to her, who was the captivating fortune of the world.
Once, playing in a garden grove, the very charming girl / saw a delightful pair of male and female parrots conversing.
They were exceedingly joyful, passionately enamored of love, / and speaking to one another with affection in pleasing voices.
Sporting at that time, the pair flew swiftly into the sky / and, resting upon a mountain ridge, made these sounds:
'Rāma will be an attractive king on earth; / and his wife will indeed be named Sītā.
With her, the wise and mighty one will rule the kingdom / for eleven thousand years, subduing other kings.
Blessed is that Queen Jānakī, and blessed is he named Rāma, / who, having obtained each other, will rejoice with delight upon earth!'
As the pair of parrots were conversing thus, the daughter of Mithilā, / recognising this pair to be deities and observing their speech,
'This pair of parrots is relating charming stories about me! / Catching them, I will ask all about the meaning behind their words.'
Having reflected thus, she said to her female companions: / 'Catch this lovely pair of birds gently!'
Those female companions, going to that mountain, caught the excellent pair of birds / and presented it out of a desire to please their friend.
Seeing them uttering manifold sounds and looking charming, / she consoled them and then asked these words:
Sītā said: / 'Do not fear, you lovely two! Who are you, and whence have you come? / Who is Rāma, and who is that Sītā? From where was that knowledge remembered?
Tell me all that quickly, so that your fear of me may depart!' / Thus questioned by her, the pair of birds related everything.
The pair of birds said: / 'There is a great sage, Vālmīki, foremost among knowers of dharma; / we two dwell constantly in his delightful hermitage.
That sage, devoted to the welfare of all beings, had his disciples sing / the future Rāmāyaṇa every day, recalling its verses.
Then by us two, that whole great future Rāmāyaṇa was heard; / being sung repeatedly, it came to us by continuous recitation.
Listen, we two will tell you who Rāma is and who Jānakī is, / and whatever will happen to her through Rāma, whose spirit delights in play.
In the sacrifice performed by Ṛṣyaśṛṅga, Hari, divided fourfold, / will manifest as the glorious Lord whose noble stories are sung by celestial women.
Along with Kauśika and his brother, he will reach Mithilā, / and then, holding the bow in hand that is hard for other kings to grasp,
having broken the bow, he will win the charming daughter of Janaka; / together with her he will rule a vast kingdom—so it was heard, O fair lady!
This and other things were heard by us who were present there and flew up. / It has been told to you, O lovely-limbed one; release us who wish to go!'
taking into her ears their speech which was most delightful, / spoke these words once more to the pair of birds:
“Where does that Rāma reside? Whose son is he? How will that best of men / take her [in marriage]? What sort of form does he bear?
Tell everything that I have asked just as it is! / Afterwards, I will do all that is pleasant and delightful to you.”
Hearing that, and seeing that she was tormented by desire, / that female parrot, knowing in her heart that she was Jānakī, recited before her then:
“The banner of the Solar dynasty, wise and mighty is King Daśaratha, / relying upon whom the gods will completely conquer all their enemies.
He will have three wives, bearing beauty that enchants Śakra; / in them there will be a quartet of offspring, lofty in power.
Rāma is the eldest of them all; Bharata is remembered next to him; / after him is glorious Lakṣmaṇa; [and] Śatrughna is powerful in every way.

The high-minded one will attain fame as ‘Raghunātha’; / infinite are the names of that mighty Rāma, O friend!

His handsome face is like the bud of a lotus; / his eyes are like lotuses, exceedingly long;

his nose is raised, broad, and charming; / his eyebrows are pleasingly joined and delightful;

his charming arms reach down to his knees; / his neck is short and adorned like a conch;

this spotless chest, bearing the auspicious mark, / has an expanse as broad as an excellent door-panel;

his thighs are lovely, accompanied by the beauty of his waist, / and his pair of knees are flawless and well-formed.
the lotus-feet of the lord of the Raghus, exceedingly radiant, / are perpetually served by all his own followers.
Rāma possesses such a form; yet how can he be described by me? / Even a hundred-faced being does not reach [the end]; how much less birds like me!
Beholding his form, Lakṣmī, bearing a graceful and charming body, / was infatuated; who is there on earth that is not infatuated?
He is of great strength, great valour, bearing a form of supreme enchantment; / how can I describe Śrī Rāma, endowed with all lordly powers and virtues?
Blessed is that Queen Jānakī, bearing a form of supreme enchantment, / who, united with him, will delight joyfully for ten thousand years.
Who are you? What is your name, ah, beautiful one, that you / skillfully inquire of me with reverence about the praise of Rāma?”
Hearing this speech of the two birds, Jānakī / spoke, declaring her charming, delightful birth:
“I am that very Jānakī, daughter of Janaka, of whom you spoke. / When that very delightful Rāma comes and takes me,
then indeed I will release you both, not otherwise; lured by your words, / I shall cherish you. Let the two sweet-voiced ones stay happily in my house!”
Hearing what she had said, both of them trembled and were gripped with fear; / agitated with one another, they spoke to Jānakī:
“We are indeed birds, O virtuous lady, forest-dwellers moving in trees; / we roam everywhere; we will have no happiness in a house.
I am pregnant; having gone to my own place and given birth to my children, / I will come to your place; truly spoken is my word!”
Though spoken to in this way by her, she did not release the female parrot. / Then her husband, anxious, spoke to her in a humble manner:
“O Sītā, release my charming wife! Why do you keep her? / Let the two of us go to the forest; we wander happily in the woods.
My delightful wife is indeed pregnant; / having delivered her [children], I will come to you, O lovely one!”
Thus addressed, she replied to him: 'Go in happiness, O wise one! / I shall protect this happy one who brings me delight at my side.'
Thus addressed, the bird became sorrowful and spoke to her with compassion: / 'What is proclaimed by yogins is indeed true speech.'
‘One should not speak, one should not speak; let them abide in silence! / Otherwise, through the fault of speech, a rutting elephant meets the tying-post.’
If we had not spoken words here on the tree, / how would there be captivity for the two of us? Therefore, one should practice silence!”
Having spoken thus, he said to her: 'O beautiful one, I cannot live / without this wife of mine; therefore, O Sītā, charming lady, release her!'
Though advised with many kinds of words, she did not release her then. / Angered and distressed, the wife cursed Janaka’s daughter:
“Just as you separate me from my husband from this place, / even so may you, while pregnant, be separated from Rāma!”
While she, sorrowful, was speaking thus again and again, / her vital breaths departed out of grief, filled with sorrow for her husband.
As she remembered ‘Rāma, Rāma’ and spoke it again and again, / a celestial chariot arrived, and the female bird shone, gone to heaven.
When she died, her husband, that king of birds, afflicted with grief, / attained supreme anger and, heartbroken, fell into the Jāhnavī.
“Let me be born in the city of Rāma, filled with people! / By my words may she be distressed, exceedingly grieved by separation!”
Having spoken thus, sorrowful, angry, terrified, / and trembling from separation from her, he fell into the waters of the Jāhnavī adorned with whirlpools.
Due to anger, due to grief, and because of insulting Sītā, / he reached the lowest caste, becoming a washerman named Krodhana.
Even an excellent twice-born man who, out of anger, acting wickedly toward the great, / casts away his own life, goes, when dead, to the lowest caste.
That came to pass: by the words of the washerman she was slandered and separated; / and by the curse of the washerman, separated, she went to the forest.
This has been told to you, O brāhmaṇa, which you asked concerning the daughter of Videha. / Now hear the subsequent account here; I shall narrate it.

5.58.m: Śeṣa said: / Seeing Bharata unconscious, Raghunātha was exceedingly grieved. / He said this to the doorkeeper: “Bring Śatrughna to me quickly!”
Hearing that word spoken, in an instant he brought Śatrughna / to where his brother Rāma stayed together with Bharata.
Seeing Bharata unconscious and Raghunātha grieved, / [Śatrughna] bowed down, and distressed, said: “What is this great and dreadful thing?”
Then Rāma [repeated] the words spoken by the outcaste, reviled by the world; / that Rāma spoke to him, to Śatrughna who served his feet,
his face cast down, his voice plaintive, with faltering syllables and trembling: / “Listen, brother, to my word today, and do it quickly with respect!”
"So that my stainless fame may spread over the earth like the Gaṅgā, / having heard the incomparable reproach against Sītā spoken in the world by the outcaste,
I wish to abandon my own body, or indeed this Jānakī." / Having heard this statement of Rāma, that slayer of foes,
trembling, pained, the crusher of enemies fell upon the ground. / Regaining consciousness after a moment, he said to the lord of the Raghus:
Śatrughna said: / "What is this harsh thing that is being said regarding Jānakī, O master? / When reviled by heretics, evil-minded men, and those outcast from all dharma,
does the Veda become unacceptable to the twice-born? / The Jāhnavī destroys sins and takes away evil for all the worlds;
if touched by sinful men, is its touch no longer honored by the virtuous? / Ah, the sun rises in the world to illuminate the world;
if it does not produce delight for owls, what loss is there in that? / Therefore, take her back! Do not abandon an unblemished woman!
O venerable Rāma, out of compassion, carry out my word!" / Hearing that speech of that great-souled Śatrughna,
he repeated again and again what he had said to Bharata. / Having heard that word of his brother, overwhelmed by a flood of sorrow,
he fell unconscious to the ground like a tree cut down at the root. / Seeing his brother Śatrughna fallen, exceedingly afflicted,
he said this to the door-keeper: "Bring Lakṣmaṇa near!" / He went to Lakṣmaṇa's house and reported this statement:
The door-keeper said: / "Master, Rāma is indeed summoning you with haste." / Hearing that summons from Rāmacandra, with haste
he went swiftly to that place where the sinless one was with his brother. / Seeing Bharata unconscious and Śatrughna also unconscious,
and venerable Rāmacandra stricken with grief, he, grieved, spoke these words: / "What is this dreadful thing seen, O king, such as fainting and the like?
Tell me everything immediately, especially the primary cause, O sinless one!" / To him speaking thus, the king told the whole account from the beginning
swiftly to Lakṣmaṇa, [himself] overwhelmed by a flood of sorrow. / Lakṣmaṇa, having heard that speech concerning the abandonment of Sītā,
sighing and breathing repeatedly, became as if his limbs were paralyzed. / Seeing his brother whose limbs were paralyzed, trembling again and again,
and saying nothing at all, [Rāma], afflicted with sorrow, said: / "What shall I do, remaining on earth, branded with ill fame?
Out of fear of the world and filled with sorrow, I will abandon this glorious body. / Always my brothers were eager to carry out my command;
now, by fate, even they speak contrary words! / Where shall I go? To whom shall I turn? Kings on earth will laugh at me,
spotted with ill fame, just as handsome men laugh at a leper. / In the lineage of Manu, kings born in ancient times were each endowed with superior virtues;
now that I am born, however, the opposite has occurred!" / Seeing venerable Rāma speaking in this way, he,
holding back his profuse tears, said with a faltering voice: / "O master, do not despair! How has your mind been stolen away?
Who indeed abandons the unblemished Sītā? You are learned in the scriptures. / I shall summon the washerman and question him:
'How was she, Jānakī, best of women, reviled by you?' / In your country, even an insignificant person is not harmed by force;
therefore, act in such a way that conviction arises in his heart! / For what reason is this timid woman, devoted to her vow to her husband, being abandoned?
In mind and speech, the daughter of Janaka knows no other! / Therefore, accept her; do not abandon this Jānakī!
Taking pity upon me, follow quickly what I have said!" / To him speaking thus, Rāma, emaciated by grief,
answered Lakṣmaṇa, instructing him with words of dharma, steadfast in his resolve to abandon her.
Rāma said: / "Why do you say to me: 'Do not abandon this unblemished woman'? / Because of the censure of the world I will abandon her, even though I know she is sinless.
For the sake of my own fame, I would abandon my own unworthy body; / I would even abandon you, my brother, if censured by popular talk,
how much more other things: houses, sons, friends, and splendid wealth? / For the sake of my own fame, I abandon everything; how much more the princess of Mithilā?
Neither my brother, nor my wife, nor my kinsmen are as dear to me / as my stainless fame, renowned in the world, is dear.
Now the washerman should certainly not be questioned. / In time, everything will happen to delight the hearts of the people.
Just as a disease when it is unripened cannot be treated on earth, / but in time, through maturation and medicine, it is destroyed,
so in time it will come about; at present, do not delay! / Abandon this virtuous woman in the forest, or slay me with a sword!"
Hearing these words spoken, the great Lakṣmaṇa / then became distressed and, consumed with sorrow, reflected in his heart.
"Commanded by his father, the son of Jamadagni even killed his mother. / An elder's command is never to be transgressed, whether proper or improper in every way.
Therefore, I will certainly abandon her out of a desire to please Rāma." / Reflecting thus in his mind, he spoke to his brother:
Lakṣmaṇa said: / "Even that which is not to be done must be done; one should never transgress an elder's command. / Therefore, I will do your bidding, whatever you say, O you of noble vows!"
To Lakṣmaṇa who was speaking thus, he replied: / 'Well done! Well done, O wise one! You have pleased my mind.'
This very night, Jānakī has a pregnancy longing to see female ascetics. / On that pretext, having placed her on a chariot, release her in the great forest!"
Hearing what was said in this manner, his face drying up completely, / weeping and shedding tears, he went to his own dwelling.
Summoning Sumantra, he then spoke these words to him: / "Prepare a chariot for me, adorned with excellent horses!"
Hearing his command, he then brought the chariot. / Seeing that chariot brought, Lakṣmaṇa, afflicted with grief,
experiencing supreme sorrow, mounted the excellent chariot / and, sighing, the servant of his brother set out for Jānakī's house.
Having gone into the inner quarters, the brother of Rāma, / sighing, addressed the daughter of Mithilā with words, overwhelmed by a flood of sorrow:
"Mother Jānakī, I have been sent by Rāma to your dwelling. / Go to the female ascetics in order to fulfill your pregnancy longing!"
Hearing these words of Lakṣmaṇa, the daughter of Videha, / filled with the highest joy, spoke to Lakṣmaṇa:
Jānakī said: / "Blessed am I, the queen of Mithilā, mindful of the feet of Rāma, / for the fulfillment of whose pregnancy longing he has dispatched Lakṣmaṇa!
Today, I shall bow down to the charming female ascetics living in the forest, devoted to their husbands, / and I will honor them with garments."
Having spoken thus, [she offered] delightful garments and costly ornaments, / gems, pure pearls, and fragrances such as camphor.
and sandalwood and other diverse items by the thousands, / the wife of the lord of the Raghus took, wishing to please herself.
Sītā, having repeatedly placed all these in the hands of her maidservants, / going toward Lakṣmaṇa, stumbled at that moment upon the threshold.
Not reflecting upon that out of eagerness, she said to Lakṣmaṇa, who acted for her welfare: / 'Where is that chariot by which you will convey me?'"
Sighing, he mounted the golden chariot together with Jānakī. / He said to Sumantra, “Urge the horses forward, swift as thought.”
At Lakṣmaṇa’s word, he urged on the well-yoked chariot, / constantly looking at Lakṣmaṇa, whose face was filled with tears.
Struck by his whip, his horses collapsed on the path; / when the horses would not move, he spoke to Lakṣmaṇa.
Sumantra said: / “Master, the horses do not move, though driven with effort. / What shall I do? I do not know the cause of the horses’ collapse.”
To him who spoke thus, Lakṣmaṇa replied with a choked voice: / “Summon courage, charioteer, and strike them with whips and the like!”
Hearing this speech, the driver somehow set them moving. / Then Jānakī's right eye twitched, portending misfortune.
At that very moment sorrow arose in her heart, foreboding distress; / at that very moment holy birds began to wheel around [to the left].
Seeing this, Vaidehī spoke to her brother-in-law: / “Why do I feel this urge to go and see ascetic women, best of Raghus?
May all be well with Rāma, or with Bharata and the younger brother; / and among his subjects everywhere may there be no misfortunes!”
Looking upon Jānakī speaking in this way, Lakṣmaṇa / said nothing at all, his throat choked and filled with tears.
As she went along, seeing deer passing to the left, / bringing a mass of sorrow, she spoke:
“That the deer now turn to the left of me is only to be expected; / it is quite fitting for one who is going away leaving the feet of Śrī Rāma.
The highest duty of women is the worship of their husband’s feet; / leaving that, whatever happens to me as I go elsewhere is only proper.”
While she was thus pondering the truth on the path, / the goddess Jāhnavī, attended solely by crowds of sages, was seen by her—
in whom billows of water look like milk, / in whom a wave appears bearing the form of a stairway to heaven,
from the touch of a single drop of whose water the mass of great sins / flees, finding no place [to remain] on any side.
Having reached the Gaṅgā, the son of Sumitrā, with tears pouring down, / said to Jānakī who was seated in the chariot: “Come, Sītā, down to the ground from the chariot.”
Hearing his word, Sītā swiftly descended; / held by the arm by Lakṣmaṇa, she stumbled on the thorns along the path.

5.59.m: Śeṣa said: / Then, having crossed the Jāhnavī by boat, / Lakṣmaṇa took Jānakī by the hand on the farther bank and entered the forest.
Walking on the path, she was seen with a parched face, / her delicate feet pierced by thorns, stumbling at every step.
Executing Rāghava’s command, Lakṣmaṇa then / led her into the terrible, misery-inflicting forest,
where the trees were terrifying—acacias, dense khadiras, / śleṣmātakas, and tamarinds—withered by forest fire;
where great serpents staying in tree-hollows hiss furiously, / and where screech-owls shriek, striking terror into the hearts of men;
where ferocious tigers, lions, jackals, and leopards are seen, / as well as straightforward, exceedingly fierce man-eaters;
where wicked buffaloes and boars, marked by two tusks, / wild with frenzy, cause torment to the minds of living beings.
Beholding such a forest, overcome with fever from fear, / her feet bitten by thorns, she spoke these words to Lakṣmaṇa:
Jānakī said: / “O hero, I do not see the eye-delighting hermitages frequented by ṛṣis and munis, / nor their wives whose wealth is great austerity.
I see only ferocious birds and dried-up trees, / and this entire forest being consumed by a forest fire.
And I see you afflicted with sorrow, your eyes filled and troubled with tears; / at every step there befalls me a thousand ill omens.
Therefore tell me, best of heroes, why have I of wicked heart been abandoned / by the great-souled Rāma? Tell me quickly what is true!”
Hearing these words, Lakṣmaṇa, consumed by grief, / his face choked with tears, said nothing at that time.
Still traversing that terrifying forest accompanied by Lakṣmaṇa, / she, afflicted with sorrow, again looked upon the stricken face of the hero.
Even then he did not speak to her, eager only to look at her; / then she insistently questioned him with extreme persistence.
When questioned with insistence by Sītā, Lakṣmaṇa, / his throat choked, grieving again and again, spoke of the abandonment.
Hearing that speech like a thunderbolt, O best of sages, / she fell like a fine creeper severed at the root, devoid of consciousness.
At that very moment the earth did not swallow this daughter of hers, / fearing: ‘May Rāma not abandon Sītā, who is sinless!’
Seeing Vaidehī fallen, the son of Sumitrā was distressed; / with a breeze fanned by the tips of sprouts, he restored her to consciousness.
Having regained consciousness, she said: “Do not mock me, brother-in-law! / How could that best of Raghus abandon me, who am free from sin?
Having lamented much in this way, seeing Lakṣmaṇa overwhelmed with sorrow, / she fainted and fell to the ground in deep distress.
Regaining consciousness after a moment, flooded with grief, / wounded by sorrow, remembering Rāma's feet, she said:
“How can the noble Raghunātha, of great intellect, abandon me— / he who for my sake built a bridge across the ocean with the monkeys?
How will that great hero abandon me, who am sinless, / on the word of a washerman? In this matter fate alone has turned against me!”
Speaking thus, the daughter of Videha fell into a swoon once more. / Seeing her fainted, he then wept with a broken voice.
Regaining consciousness again, she spoke thus to the son of Sumitrā, / deeply distressed, seeing him afflicted with grief with a choked throat:
“O son of Sumitrā, go to Rāma, the embodiment of dharma, the treasury of fame; / speak these very words of mine in the presence of that treasury of austerities:
‘That you have abandoned me, knowing that I am sinless— / is that worthy of your lineage, or is it the fruit of knowledge of the scriptures?
I was ever devoted to your feet, eating only the remnants of your meal; / that you have abandoned me—fate alone is the cause of it all.
May prosperity be yours everywhere, best among the foremost heroes! / As for me, remembering you in the forest, I shall maintain my life.
In mind, deed, and speech, you alone are my supreme lord; / all others have been deemed worthless by my mind, O scion of Raghu!
In birth after birth, may you alone be my husband, O lord of the earth; / through remembrance of your feet, sins are destroyed, O ruler of virtuous wives!’
Deliver my entire message to all the mothers-in-law, best of Raghus: / ‘A sinless, chaste wife has been abandoned in the terrible forest by Rāma.
I remember your feet in the forest filled with herds of wild beasts; / pregnant, I have been abandoned in the forest by the great-souled Rāma.’
O son of Sumitrā, hear my words: may good fortune attend the best of Raghus! / I now relinquish my life, guarding Rāma's progeny.”
Since you carry out Rāma's word truly, may good befall you; / that deed must be done by one under another's command who serves Rāma's lotus feet.
Go to Rāma's presence; may your paths indeed be auspicious! / Compassion should be shown to me; I ought to be remembered from time to time."
Having spoken thus, she then fell unconscious to the ground before him; / seeing Jānakī swooning, Lakṣmaṇa was overcome with sorrow.
He fanned her with the corners of his garments, and when she naturally regained consciousness, / the son of Sumitrā consoled her again and again with sweet words.
Lakṣmaṇa said: / "Here, indeed, I go to Rāma; having gone, I shall report everything. / Near you is the great hermitage of the sage Vālmīki."
Having spoken thus and circumambulated her, sorrowful and filled with tears, / shedding drops of tears from grief, he went to King Rāma.
The daughter of Janaka, looking at her departing brother-in-law with astonished eyes, [thought:] / "Is he laughing, this highly fortunate Lakṣmaṇa, my brother-in-law?
How did Rāghava abandon me, dearer than life, sinless?" / Thinking thus, she gazed at him with unblinking eyes.
Realizing that he had completely crossed the Jāhnavī and that her abandonment was true, / she fell down, imperiled in life, and then fell into a swoon.
Then swans, bringing water from all sides with their wings, / sprinkled [her], and a sweet wind blew, fragrant with flowers.
Elephants came, as if washing with their trunks / full of water from all sides her body covered in dust.
Deer approached near her and stood with wondering eyes; / trees became filled with blossoms at that time, though out of season.
When this took place at that time, the virtuous woman regained consciousness; / smitten with deep sorrow, she lamented, crying, "Rāma, Rāma!"
"Ah, lord! Ah, friend of the wretched! O presence full of compassion! / Why do you abandon me in the forest without any fault?
Speaking thus, lamenting again and again, / looking here and there, and swooning repeatedly,
then the venerable Vālmīki, having entered the forest with his disciples, / heard weeping there, uttered in a plaintive voice.
He then said to his disciples: "Look into the middle of the forest! / Who is weeping in the terrifyingly dreadful forest with a sorrowful voice?"
Sent by the sage, they went to where the daughter of Janaka was, / calling "Rāma, Rāma!", overwhelmed by a flood of tears.
Seeing that woman, they returned eagerly to the sage Vālmīki; / having heard the words spoken by them, the sage then went there.
Seeing that heap of austerities, the daughter of Janaka, devoted to her husband, [said:] / "Salutation to the sage, the embodiment of the Veda, the ocean of vows!"
He greeted Sītā, who had spoken thus, with blessings: / 'Live long with your husband, and obtain two splendid sons!'
Who are you, and why have you come to the dreadful forest in such a state? / Tell me everything, so that I may know the cause of your sorrow."
Then she, Rāma's wife, replied to this sage, / sighing, with a plaintive voice, trembling:
"Hear my meaningful word, the cause of all my sorrow; / know me to be the servant of Raghunātha, the lord of the earth.
Abandoned without a fault, I do not know the reason for it; / Lakṣmaṇa left me here and went away by Rāghava's command."
Consoling the lotus-eyed Jānakī, who having spoken thus / had her lotus face filled with drops of tears, Vālmīki said:
"Know me to be Vālmīki, the sage, the guru of your father. / Do not grieve, O Vaidehī; come indeed to my hermitage.
Know it to be your father's home in a different place, O woman devoted to her husband; / in such an act, my anger is indeed directed against the king."
Hearing this speech, the daughter of Janaka, devoted to her husband, / her face covered in tears of sorrow, attained some comfort.
Śeṣa said: / Having consoled her whose eyes were agitated by a flood of sorrow, / Vālmīki led her to his holy hermitage, filled with a gathering of female ascetics.
Walking behind this Vālmīki, the treasure of austerities, / she shone like a charming star behind the moon.
Having reached his own hermitage filled with sages, Vālmīki / announced to the female ascetics that the daughter of Janaka had arrived at his hermitage.
Vaidehī, noble-minded, bowed to all the female ascetics; / highly delighted, they embraced one another.
Vālmīki, the treasure of austerities, spoke to his disciples: / "Ah, let a charming leaf-hut be built for the daughter of Janaka!"
Hearing these most delightful words of Vālmīki, / they constructed a very charming hut with leaves and wood.
There Vaidehī dwelt, devoted to her duty to her husband, / rendering service to Vālmīki and subsisting on fruits.
Chanting "Rāma, Rāma" herself in mind and speech, / the daughter of Janaka, devoted to her husband, spent the days there.
In due time, that daughter of Janaka gave birth to two sons possessing charming bodies, / veritable representations of Rāmacandra, like the two Aśvins.
Hearing of the birth of the sons of Janaka's daughter, the sage, delighted / and foremost among knowers of mantras, performed the birth rites and other ceremonies.
The sage Vālmīki performed the rites with kuśa grass and lava grass; / clearly after their names the appellation of the two sons became Kuśa and Lava.
Because Vālmīki, free of taint, performed the auspicious rite in that way, / that lotus-eyed woman became exceedingly joyful in heart.
On that day, having slain Lavaṇa, Śatrughna with a small army / arrived at this hermitage of Vālmīki in the pleasant night.
Then Śatrughna was instructed by Vālmīki: "Do not tell / the leader of the Raghus about the two sons of Janaka's daughter; I shall speak [of them] later."
There the two charming sons of Janaka's daughter grew up; / nourished on roots, tubers, and fruits, he made the two excellent boys spirited.
Very charming like the moon of the first day of the bright fortnight, / in time the two charming boys received their sacraments and were invested with the sacred thread.

Having invested them with the sacred thread, the sage taught the two sons the Veda along with its limbs; / he taught them the science of archery with its esoteric secrets, and made them recite the Rāmāyaṇa.
And Vālmīki gave the two of them two bows, well adorned with gold, / unbreakable, strung, excellent, capable of rending hosts of foes.
He then gave the two sons of Janaka's daughter two quivers filled with arrows, / two inexhaustible scimitars, and unbreakable shields.
Bearing bows and having mastered the science of archery, moving about joyfully in the hermitage, / the two shone there, splendid like the two Aśvins.
Seeing her two excellent sons bearing swords and shields, / the daughter of Janaka attained supreme joy and gave up that [grief] born of separation.
This has been related to you, O brāhmaṇa: the birth of the sons of Janaka's daughter; / now hear what happened—the severing of the arms of the heroes.

5.60.m: Śeṣa said: / Śatrughna, beholding the severed arms of his own warriors, / spoke to them, highly enraged, biting his lower lip in wrath.

"By which hero were your arms cut off and not made equal, oh?
I shall cut off the arms of that one, though protected by the gods, O soldiers!

That great fool does not know the vast might of Rāmacandra.
Now I will show my own strength with overwhelming power.

Where is that hero? Where is that delightful horse?
Or who is the fool that seized sleeping serpents, knowing their prowess?"
Thus addressed, the warriors, astonished and deeply grieved, / praised the boy who was the exact likeness of Rāmacandra.

Hearing of the horse's capture by a boy, his eyes reddened with fury;
eager to fight, he commanded the army general, Kālajit:
