"O general, marshal the entire army by my command!
We must advance against the enemy now, who possesses great strength and prowess.

This is surely no mere boy holding the horse—he must be Hari,
or he may be Tripura's enemy; otherwise, none could take my horse away.

Inevitably, a great slaughter of the mighty army will take place.
Sporting with unrestrained deeds, the child sits fearless in mind.

Equipped for battle, invincible to enemies, we must go there."
Having heard these words of Śatrughna, the army commander

readied that fourfold army, formidable in its array.
Seeing it prepared, excellent and accompanied by the four divisions,

Śatrujit ordered them to advance to where the boy holding the horse was.
Then that army marched, accompanied by its four divisions,

shaking the surface of the earth, terrifying the enemies by force.
Then the general saw the boy who had the form of Rāma.

Reflecting on his resemblance to Rāma, he spoke beneficial words:
"O boy, release the excellent horse of the mighty Rāma!

I am the general named Kālajit, fiercely proud, belonging to that king.
Seeing you resembling Rāma, compassion arises in my heart.

Otherwise, because of your insolence, there will be no life left for you."
Indeed, hearing these words of the soldier of Śatrughna,

he laughed slightly out of anger and spoke wonderful words:
"Go, you are spared! Tell that Rāma about the horse's capture.

I do not fear you, O warrior, despite your prudent words.
I take no account of you here, even if there are ten million like you!

By the grace of my mother's feet, they will become like cotton, no doubt.
As for your name Kālajit, made up of pretty syllables,

it is like the ripe bimba fruit in color only, not in power.
Show your valor now, marked by the strength of your own name!

Having conquered me, your death, your name will be true."
Śeṣa said:
Pierced by words like thunderbolts, that crest-jewel of good warriors

became exceedingly enraged in heart and spoke these words once more:
"In what lineage is your birth? What is your name, O boy?
I do not know your name, your family, your character, nor your age.

I am mounted on a chariot; how can I conquer a foot-soldier through unrighteousness?"
Then, exceedingly enraged, [Lava] spoke these words again:

"What use is lineage, character, or a delightful name?
I am Lava; bit by bit, I shall conquer all the enemy soldiers.

Now I will make you, soldier, a foot-traveler as well!"
Having spoken thus, the mighty Lava strung his bow

and then twanged it, striking fear into the hearts of the warriors.
Lava, first remembering Vālmīki and his mother Jānakī,

released sharp arrows that instantly took life away.
Kālajit, stringing his own bow, filled with anger,

the swift one, skilled in battle, struck Lava.
Slicing his arrows into a hundred pieces swiftly in an instant, Kuśa's younger brother

deprived the general of his chariot with eight of his own excellent arrows.
Rendered chariotless, he mounted an elephant brought by his own soldiers,

maddened with rut, of great speed, flowing with juice in seven streams.
Seeing him mounted on the elephant, smiling, the conqueror of all enemy hosts

pierced him with ten arrows discharged from his bow.
Seeing his valor, Kālajit was astonished in mind,

and hurled a huge mace forged of great iron.
As that mace came rushing swiftly, made from ten thousand bhāras of metal,

Kuśa's younger brother quickly cut it into three pieces with crescent-tipped arrows.
A sharp, terrifying iron club, raised to take the enemy's life,

was hurled again by him, and Lava swiftly cut it to pieces.
Having severed that dread club, his eyes red with anger,

he was enraged, thinking of him mounted on the elephant's back.
Instantly he severed the tusker's trunk with his sword;

placing his feet on its two tusks, he climbed onto the elephant's head.
Splitting the [general's] crown into a hundred pieces and his armor into a thousand,

he dragged the commander by his hair and dashed him to the ground.
Cast down from the elephant's back, the general grew enraged again,

and struck [Lava] on the chest with a fist hard as an adamantine fist.
Though struck with fists, [Lava], his bow bent into a circle,

quickly released sharp crescent-tipped arrows into his chest.
He shone on the edge of the battlefield with his bow bent in a circle,

wearing a helmet and armor impenetrable to ten million arrows.
Pierced by sharp shafts, [the general] took up a sword to kill him,

gnashing his teeth in fury, breathing heavily again and again.
As that heroic commander approached with sword in hand, Lava

severed the middle of his arm, and the hand fell with the sword.
Seeing his hand holding the sword severed, the army leader out of rage

began to strike him with a club in his left hand.
That arm of his too, adorned with an armlet, was cut off by sharp arrows.

Then, enraged, the warrior struck Lava with his feet.
Struck by his foot, Lava did not budge on the battlefield;

just like an elephant struck by a garland, he severed his legs.
Even then, he began to strike him with his head.

Then Lava, judging the army commander to possess excessive bravery,
took in hand a scimitar resembling the fire of destruction at the end of time,

and cut off his head, which was adorned with a great crest.
A great cry of woe arose when the commander of the army was felled.

The soldiers, utterly infuriated, advanced to kill Lava;
Lava, with the strikes of his arrows, turned them to flight.

Some had their limbs severed and pierced; some departed from the battlefield.
Having checked all the warriors, he happily plunged into the army,

like the Boar breathing deeply in the vast ocean during the cosmic dissolution.
Elephants were split in two, and the earth was covered with pearls;

it became impassable to the foremost warriors, as though covered with mountains.
Horses with golden saddles, radiant and adorned with jewels,

fell, scorched with blood, into the pool, glorious in their strength.
Chariot-fighters, splendid with bow-staffs held in the middle of their hands,

fell onto the floor of their chariots, just like gods descending from heaven.
With lips bitten, marked by the roving fortune of battle on their faces,

the warriors skilled in battle were seen fallen there.
A river of blood flowed, with horses' heads as turtles,

charming with its mighty current, causing terror to enemies.
The arms of some were cut off; the feet of some were severed;

the ears and noses of some, and the armor and earrings of others.
Thus, indeed, a slaughter occurred when the army commander fell in battle.
All the heroes fell; not a single one survived from there. / Having achieved victory in battle and conquered the host of enemies,
Lava looked around, keeping his mind watchful of any other arrival. / A few who survived the battle, who had not died in the fight by good fortune,
went into the presence of Śatrughna to announce the wondrous event. / Having gone, they related what had occurred on the battlefield:
the slaying of Kālajit by a boy, and his astounding enterprise in battle. / Hearing that, Śatrughna was seized with wonder, and he spoke to them,
laughing in fury, biting his teeth, remembering the boy seizing the horse: / “O heroes! Are you mad with intoxication, or are you inventing excuses?
Or has cowardice overcome you? How could Kālajit meet his death— / he who in combat was fierce to hosts of enemies, victorious in battle?
How could a mere boy conquer him, who was unassailable even to Yama?” / Having heard Śatrughna's words, the heroes, drenched in blood, said:
“We are not drunken with intoxication, nor is this a trick, nor gambling. / Know that Kālajit’s death at the hands of Lava is the truth, O king!
And the entire army was crushed by the boy possessed of peerless valor. / Henceforth, what must be done, and what foremost of kings should be dispatched?
Thinking he is a boy, do not commit a reckless display of force here.” / Hearing these words of those heroes, the slayer of his foes then
spoke to Sumati, foremost in wisdom, concerning the battle.

5.61.m: Śatrughna said: / “Do you know, O great minister, what boy has seized the horse, / by whom my entire army, vast as an ocean, has been destroyed?”
Sumati said: / “O Lord, this is the great hermitage of Vālmīki, foremost of sages. / No kṣatriyas live here at all, O tormentor of foes!
It might be Indra, highly indignant, who seized the horse, / or the enemy of Tripura [Śiva]; otherwise, who could carry off your mount?
By whom Kālajit was met with utter destruction, most terrible— / against him, O glorious great king, who else can march other than Puṣkala?
And you, surrounded by all the valiant warriors and kings, / go there with your great army, O destroyer of enemies!
Having gone and captured the hero alive, I will show him / to Rāma, who wishes for this wonder; this is my considered opinion.”
Hearing these words, he commanded all the heroes: / 'Go with the vast army; I shall follow behind.'
Thus commanded, the heroes went instantly to where the mighty Lava was. / There he stood, stringing his very sturdy bow and drawing its cord tight.
Seeing that great army coming, filled with warriors, / the mighty Lava was not the least bit afraid in his mind.
Lava stood up like a lion, considering all the soldiers as deer, / bending his bow in fury and releasing arrows by the thousands.
Tormented by his arrows, yet filled with immense fury, / considering him only a heroic boy, they then charged straight against him.
Seeing thousands of heroes positioned all around in encircling rings, / Lava, filled with fury, quickly fitted his arrows.
The first ring was of a thousand; the second numbered ten thousand; / the third was of twenty thousand; the fourth was of fifty thousand;
the fifth was of one hundred thousand warriors; the sixth exceeded ten thousand warriors; / the seventh was of two hundred thousand—thus he was enclosed by seven rings.
In the middle, Lava, engulfed by the ring, moving about like fire, / burned all the soldiers who formed the rings.
One with swords, another with arrows, another with javelins and lances, / with axes and iron clubs—every encircling ring was shattered by the noble youth.
Freed from the seven rings, Kuśa's younger brother shone resplendent, / like the moon released from a mass of clouds at the arrival of autumn.
He struck down the warriors on every side, severing many trunks of elephants, / slicing off the heads of heroes, along with large wheel-like eyebrows.
Many heroes fell, severely afflicted by Lava's arrows; / others swooned in battle, while others, utterly terrified, fled.
Seeing the army devoted to flight, tormented by Lava's arrows, / the hero named Puṣkala advanced to fight in battle.
Saying, “Halt! Halt!”, his eyes filled with wrath, / standing in a chariot adorned with fine horses, the mighty one advanced toward Lava.
Then Puṣkala, knowing supreme weapons, said to Lava: / “Stand in the chariot adorned with fine horses given by me in combat!
Why should I fight with you on foot in battle? / Therefore, stand in a chariot; then I shall fight with you!” / Hearing these words, Lava said to Puṣkala:
“If I were to fight in battle standing in a chariot given by you, / then it would be a sin for me, and victory would surely be doubtful!
We are not brāhmaṇas, O hero, devoted to accepting gifts! / We are indeed kṣatriyas, always dedicated to the act of giving.
Now I shall angrily smash your chariot, so that you too / will be on foot; afterwards you may fight!”
Hearing this speech endowed with righteousness and courage, / Puṣkala marveled in his mind for a long time, and then readied his bow.
Seeing him taking up his bow, Lava, filled with fury, / fitting an arrow, severed the bow held in his hand.
As soon as he began stringing another bow, the haughty, mighty one [Lava], / laughing aloud in battle, smashed his chariot.
Seeing his own chariot broken and his bow severed by the noble youth, / regarding him as a great hero, he rushed forward on foot in battle.
Both were bowmen heroes; both were fierce with arrows; / both were scorched with blood; both had their armors severed;
shattered by each other's arrow strikes, yet both were visible, / desiring victory, mutually seeking each other's death,
like Jayanta and Kārttikeya, or the enemy of Tripura [Śiva] and the breaker of cities [Indra]. / While the two were thus waging combat on the battlefield,
Puṣkala then spoke to the boy: “O crest-jewel of champions! / No crest-jewel of heroes like you has ever been seen by me.
Today I will cause your head to fall with sharp, well-jointed arrows! / Do not flee in combat; protect your life with restraint!”
Having spoken thus, he enclosed the heroic Lava in a cage of arrows; / Puṣkala's arrows stood covering the earth and the sky.
Standing inside the cage of arrows, Lava said to Puṣkala: / “A great feat has been done, O hero, in that you have struck me with arrows!”
Having spoken thus and cut down the volley of arrows, the hero, / skilled in fitting arrows to his bow, spoke again to Puṣkala:
“Defend yourself standing in the fight! Tormented by the strike of my arrows, / you will fall upon the surface of the earth, drenched in blood!”
Hearing this spoken, Puṣkala, seized with anger, / fought in battle against the heroic Lava of great strength.
Lava, enraged, drew instantly from his quiver a sharp arrow / that tears through enemies, like a venomous serpent in his wrath.
That blazing arrow released from Lava's bow, / aiming to pierce his heart, was swiftly severed by the son of Bharata [Puṣkala].
When that life-destroying arrow was severed by the son of Bharata in the fight, / he became exceedingly angry and took up another terrible shaft.
Discharged with a bow drawn back to the ear, that sharp arrow / pierced the heart of Puṣkala in the great battle.
Pierced in the chest by that warrior with a swift-flying arrow, / the crest-jewel of great heroes fell upon the surface of the earth.
Seeing that Puṣkala had fallen, the son of the wind, / taking him up, delivered him, filled with swoon, to Rāghava's brother.
Seeing him unconscious, his mind overwhelmed with grief, / filled with rage he directed Hanūmat to slay Lava.
Hanūmān, scorched with anger, in the fight against mighty Lava, / swiftly advanced to conquer [him], having raised up a śālmali tree.
The mighty Hanumān struck Lava on the head with the tree; / Lava swiftly cut into a hundred pieces that [tree] as it came flying down.
When the tree was cut down, having uprooted trees from their roots again in rage, / the mighty one struck [him] on the chest and head.
Whatever trees the son of the wind fetched and struck with, / all of them the mighty one swiftly severed with his straight-jointed arrows.
Then, having uprooted rocks resembling boulders, the monkey, / Māruti, hurled them down upon his head with swift speed.
Struck by masses of rocks in the battle, raising his bow, / he crushed them with arrows, just as grain [is crushed] by millstones.
Then, extremely enraged, the capable Māruti made an encirclement / with his tail around the mighty Lava on the edge of the battlefield.
Seeing himself entangled by the tail, remembering his mother in his heart, / the mighty [Lava] struck Māruti's tail with his fist.
Pained by the blow of that fist, Māruti released him; / released from the tail in battle, the mighty one kept discharging arrows.
His body tormented by the blow of irresistible arrows, the monkey, / considering that great shower of arrows unbearable in battle, [thought:]
"What should be done by us here? If [I] go away having fled, / then my master would feel shame: 'A mere boy struck me here.'"
"Because of the boon granted by Brahmā, there is neither fainting nor death [for me]; / but here the pain of arrows is unbearable. What must be done by me now?"
"Let Śatrughna go into battle and obtain victory over the boy; / I, meanwhile, desiring victory, will lie down in a feigned swoon."
Resolving thus in his mind, he feigned unconsciousness / and fell upon the battlefield while all the heroes looked on.
Perceiving that mighty Hanūmat to be unconscious, / he, skilled in shooting arrows, struck down all the kings.

5.62.m: Śeṣa said: / Hearing that Māruti had swooned, Śatrughna fell into grief: / "What should be done by me in battle? This boy is exceedingly powerful."
Standing himself in a chariot of gold along with the best of heroes, / he advanced to fight where Lava, skilled in wondrous warfare, was.
He saw Lava, who seemed like Rāma having attained childhood on earth, / holding bow and arrow in hand, throwing down heroes in the vanguard of battle.
He reflected then: "Who is this bearer of Rāma's form, / having a charming body, dark as the petal of a blue lotus?"
"This is surely the son of the daughter of the king of Videha, not otherwise; / having conquered us in battle, he will depart like a lion."
"No victory is to be ours, who are devoid of power; / being powerless, what shall we do in battle, [though] skilled in warfare?"
Having reflected thus, he then spoke words to the boy / who brought wonder to the battle and felled crores of heroes:
"Who are you, boy, that you strike down our warriors to the earth in battle? / Do you not know the might of King Rāma, the destroyer of demons?
Who is your mother, who is your father, through whose good fortune [you] attained victory? / What is your renowned name in the world? Let me know [it], O mighty one!
Release the horse! Why was it bound? Because of [your] childhood I forgive that of yours. / Come, behold Rāma; abundant [wealth] will be given to you."
Thus addressed, the heroic boy spoke to Śatrughna: / 'What is the use of a name, or a father, or lineage, or age?'
Fight in battle, hero, if you possess strength! / Having bowed to the heroic Kuśa at his feet, depart, not otherwise!
You may be the heroic brother of Rāma, [yet] not the best of the mighty among us two; / release the horse by force, if you have the power!"
Having spoken thus and fitted his arrow, the formidable one struck / him in the heart, on the head, and on both arms in the arena of battle.
Then the enraged king strung his bow, / making a sound deep as a thundercloud, as if terrifying the boy.
The best of the mighty discharged innumerable arrows; / the boy cut to pieces all those hosts of arrows by his might.
The surface of the earth was covered with arrows released in manifold ways by Lava; / like a gift offered during a vyatīpāta, they became inexhaustible.
Those arrows fitted by Lava covered the entire sky; / reaching the orb of the sun, they wheeled on all sides.
Even the wind did not enter into the reach of that cage of arrows; / what talk then of human beings, who betoken only a moment's life?
Seeing his extensive arrows, Śatrughna fell into astonishment; / skilled in discharging arrows, he severed hundreds of thousands [of them].
Seeing all those arrows of his severed, Kuśa's younger brother / swiftly cut the bow of the lord of the earth, Śatrughna.
Taking up another bow, as soon as he discharged arrows, / so soon did he shatter his chariot with sharp-jointed arrows.
He severed the very firm, strung bow held in his hand; / the heroes standing on the battlefield praised that deed.
His bow severed, his chariot gone, his horses killed, his charioteer slain, / mounting another chariot he forcefully advanced to fight Lava.
Pierced by many arrows, his body streaming with blood, / he shone in the midst of battle like a blossoming kiṃśuka tree.
Struck by Śatrughna's arrows, [Lava] attained supreme wrath; / skilled in fitting arrows, he bent his bow into a circle.
He rendered Śatrughna's body shattered of its armour, / his head devoid of its diadem, and scorched with flowing blood.
Then Rāma's younger brother, enraged, released ten sharp-pointed, / life-destroying arrows, being exceedingly infuriated.
Reducing those very [arrows] to bits like sesame seeds with his sharp-jointed arrows, / he struck Śatrughna on the chest with eight arrows.
Severely afflicted by the torment of arrows, mindful of the mighty Lava, / deeming him unbearable, he then ceased discharging arrows.
Then, by Lava, he was pierced in his broad chest with a sharp / [arrow] resembling a crescent moon and adorned with sharp joints.
Pierced in the chest by that arrow, having suffered dreadful pain, / he fell onto the lap of the chariot, bow in hand, looking splendid.
Seeing Śatrughna unconscious, the kings such as Suratha and others / rushed against Lava, striving to achieve victory in the battle then.
Suratha, the heroic Vimala, King Vīramaṇi as well, / Sumada, Riputāpa, and others surrounded [him] in the conflict.
Some with razor-headed arrows, some with clubs, some with dreadful shafts, / some with lances, and some with axes—the kings struck on all sides.
Seeing them eager to fight unrighteously, the crest-jewel of heroes / struck them in battle with ten arrows each.
Struck by the rain of arrows in the midst of battle, those very angry [kings], / some fled, and some fainted in the circle of battle.
Meanwhile, King Śatrughna, abandoning his faint in the battle, / advanced with his army to fight the great hero Lava.
Approaching him, he said to Lava: "Blessed are you, who appear as a child! / You are no child, but some god who has come to deceive me.
I was never struck down in the battle arena by any hero; / yet by you I was brought to a faint, before my very eyes.
Now behold my valour; I will strike you down in battle. / Endure this single arrow; do not run away, boy!"
Having spoken thus in the battle, he took up a single arrow against the boy, / terrible as the mouth of Yama, by which Lavaṇa had been slain.
Setting that blazing arrow and intending to pierce the heart / of Lava, who, like fire, consumed all of the thousands of heroes,
seeing that blazing arrow illuminating the ten directions, / he remembered the mighty Kuśa, who strikes down enemies:
"If at this moment my heroic and powerful brother were here, / then this terrible fear of falling under Śatrughna's power would not befall me."
While the great-souled Lava was considering thus, / the great arrow, terrible and like the fire of cosmic dissolution, struck his heart.
Struck by the king's arrow, the hero then fell into a faint / on the battlefield adorned with the heads of all the warriors.
